title: Going out to parties, meeting his wife, and the rival Invincibles
summary: After three years of practice, at about fourteen the group begins playing at girls' houses, where he meets his future wife. The better string group, the Invincibles, becomes the Owls.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Oh, I would say around 11, 12 years old. That's all. Maybe 14 years, I don't know you. Not that old. No, we didn't ever leave that house for three years. We practiced until we were about 14. Then we began going out. Now there were a lot of older men in the crowd, and I wouldn't say older. Oh yeah, I know. Maybe 15, 16, they were old compared to us. But then when I got to be about 14, then we actually ventured out and began playing on Sunday night after we'd practiced all afternoon at the Reynolds' we'd go to some girl's house, and they'd give you cokes and sandwiches and spend the whole evening. Then the thing got to be very regular, either Saturday or Sunday or both, where nobody was invited to these parties unless they could sing or play. And that's how I ran into my wife. She was a classical piano teacher, but she also played a very good jazz ragtime piano, if you will. They were already getting away from the ragtime, although I remember many of the pieces that she had was entertainers rag, the maple leaf and all those. Others were beginning to come in, and the style of playing was changing then. I don't think we ever played what really would be called ragtime. It was always. And the thing that made us compete and improve was we had a group opposite to us. There was a boy who lived right across from the Reynolds. Why the Reynolds has never invited him over, I'll never understand, because he was a better musician than any of us, and that was Bill Clappinger. He was an orphan, and he would sit alone on his porch and practice hour after hour, and those Reynolds never invited him over. Now he became one of a group that was a very fine bunch of musicians. They all knew cording and arrangements and stuff much better than we did. They would call themselves the Invincibles, and they were really a hot competition with us. They had some fine musicians in there.
Were the winds in there or just strings?

All strings, yes. All strings. I was going to tell you. Red Mackey was on bass and banjo. Frank Mackey is his name, they called him Red. Then Rene Jelpe was on banjo. They had Eblen Rau on violin, Roletishner on guitar, Monk Smith, did I mention him? No. Monk Smith on guitar and Uke. And they had about seven or eight in the crowd. But I realize now, looking back, that they really were much better than we were. But we had the pep and the zip, and we'd work up some kind of little singing things with it. Incidentally, Bill, when you said people thought I couldn't sing, they never would let me sing. They thought I sang so loud that they wouldn't let me sing. Then we had a group that sang that let me contribute that, but not otherwise. And so that's the group, the Invincibles, that became eventually the Owls. Monk Smith took up clarinet and saxophone, and he also played his guitar with the band, but with a capadastro, just like I did. And Rene Jelpe continued on his banjo. Benji White was one of their, he became a sax and clarinet player. Red Mackey switched to piano and bass after they became the Owls. And that's about all of that group that really went into the Owls. But the minute they started with wind instruments, they broke up right now.
